text:
This chapter covers soil, water, and root-related requirements for healthy jackfruit trees. On soil, the text describes jackfruit as adaptable to a range of soil types but performing best in deep, well-drained, fertile loam soils; it specifically warns against waterlogged or poorly drained sites, noting that standing water around the root zone promotes root rot and can kill even established trees, and recommends raised planting or improved drainage on heavier clay soils.

On water needs, the chapter notes that young trees need regular watering during establishment (particularly in the dry season) but that mature trees are relatively drought-tolerant once well rooted, though prolonged drought during flowering and fruit development can cause flower and young fruit drop and reduce fruit size. The text discusses irrigation timing relative to flowering/fruiting stages, recommending consistent moisture particularly during fruit swelling to avoid fruit-cracking or premature drop, while cautioning against sudden heavy watering after a dry spell (which the text associates with fruit splitting).

On roots, the chapter notes jackfruit develops a deep taproot when grown from seed, which contributes to its drought tolerance but also makes bare-root transplanting of older seedlings difficult (reinforcing the nursery-bag/container planting method recommended in the earlier propagation chapter, so the root system is disturbed as little as possible at field planting).

On fertilizer, the chapter gives general guidance on feeding young and mature trees, referencing standard compound fertilizer formulations (the text cites examples such as balanced NPK ratios, e.g., 15-15-15, alongside organic manure/compost application), applied periodically during the growing season, with the amount and frequency increased as the tree matures and comes into bearing, and adjusted around flowering and fruit development stages to support fruit set and fruit size. The chapter recommends combining chemical fertilizer with organic matter (compost, manure) rather than relying on chemical fertilizer alone, for long-term soil fertility and structure.
